title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
MACS2
Model-based Analysis for ChIP-Seq MACS2 is used to identify peaks, it operates on BAM files.

-g (Genome Size) hs for Homo sapiens
-t treatment IP file
-c control input file
-f BAM format
–nomodel (used here as this is a small dataset)

# check in correct workspace (ChIP-seq_workshop)
mkdir macs2_results
# Replicate 1
macs2 callpeak -t bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1_filtered.bam \
  -c bt2_out/Input_Control_filtered.bam \
  -f BAM -g hs -n CTCF_Rep1 --nomodel \
  --outdir macs2_results/

# Replicate 2
macs2 callpeak -t bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2_filtered.bam \
  -c bt2_out/Input_Control_filtered.bam \
  -f BAM -g hs -n CTCF_Rep2 --nomodel \
  --outdir macs2_results/
Once we have called our peaks we can add these to our IGV session, but first lets start the next step running, we will examine the sequence at our peaks for specific motifs.
These are in .narrowPeaks files, the columns are as follows:

Chromosome
Start
End
Iterative id given by MACS2
Integer score for display
Strand (irrelevant in this case)
Fold-change (fold enrichment for this peak summit against random Poisson distribution with local lambda)
log10 P-value (e.g., 17.68 is 1 x 10-17)
log10 Q-value from Benjamini–Hochberg–Yekutieli procedure
Relative summit position to peak start

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
HOMER
We will just run this on our first replicate, we are using a script from the HOMER suite of tools, we will select the top 500 peaks to speed things up.
Filtered sort by Q value
sort -k9,9nr macs2_results/CTCF_Rep1_peaks.narrowPeak | head -n 500 > macs2_results/CTCF_Rep1_top500_peaks.narrowPeak
Homer requires a FASTA file and ‘preparsed’ folder, we will just create a symbolic link to these;
ln -s /home/genomes/human/hg38/hg38.fa .
ln -s /library/training/ASD/03_HTSDAC/preparsed .
-size 200 limit -mask repeats
findMotifsGenome.pl macs2_results/CTCF_Rep1_top500_peaks.narrowPeak hg38.fa -preparsedDir preparsed/ homer_results/ -size 200 -mask -p 4
Note, If running on own machine, it would be easiest to omit the ‘-preparsedDir preparsed/’ and this will build from your hg38.fa file.
This generates a html report, ‘homerResults.html’, we should see CTCF as our best match.

While that’s running lets go back and look at out peak files in IGV.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
Visually Inspect Peak Files
Go back to your web browser and navigate to the macs2_results, here we want to download our ‘.narrowPeaks’ files
[diagram in IGV with peaks added]
Go back to the “peaks” you examined before, are the results what you expected? Can you see where the highest point of the peak is?

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
DeepTools
Deeptools contains some useful plotting tools to summarise our data, lets create a heatmap across our peaks to see how strong the signal is, we can run this for all our samples, this requires a two step process.

referencePoint centre of peak
a upstream distance from reference
b downstream distance from reference

computeMatrix reference-point \
  -S bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bw bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bw bt2_out/Input_Control.bw \
  -R macs2_results/CTCF_Rep1_peaks.narrowPeak \
  --referencePoint center \
  -a 2000 -b 2000 \
  -o CTCF_multi_matrix.gz \
  -p 4
Once the above matrix file is created we can plot and customise our heatmap, feel free to play around with the colorMap or any other parameters.
plotHeatmap -m CTCF_multi_matrix.gz \
  -out CTCF_multi_heatmap.png \
  --colorMap Reds \
  --samplesLabel "Rep 1" "Rep 2" "Input" \
  --refPointLabel "Peaks" --regionsLabel "Peaks" \
  --yAxisLabel "Average signal (BPM)" --xAxisLabel "Distance from center (bp)" --yAxisLabel "Average signal (BPM)" 

Deeptools offers a lot of plotting functions to assess short read data, take a look at the List of Tools, particularly those for QC and summaries, you should have the relevant files already.


 Key points


Peak calling
Motif Discovery
Deeptools plotting


The commands in the workflow have been run one by one but basically forms the basis of a bash script, with a small amount of tweaking this could be modified to handle multiple samples simultaneously, this along with more sophisticated methods will be covered in a later workshop. While the steps for general bioinformatics pipelines are similar the tools and parameters used are specific to the data and experiment type.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
FastQC
FastQC is a tool that provides simple quality control checks on FASTQ files and creates several exploratory plots. The command can take multiple files at once or you can use wildcards (*) to specify multiple files. Once running, it will provide a progress report for each file.
cd fastq
fastqc *.fastq.gz
FastQC generates a zip file as well as an html file for each input. The html file is the easiest file to view and contains several plots and tables that provide information about the quality of the data. The zip file contains the raw data used to generate the plots, which can be useful for further analysis or troubleshooting.
Once this is finished you can view the reports via; https://bifx-core3.bio.ed.ac.uk/~username
In your web browser, navigate to your workshop folder and the reports are under fastq ending with ’_fastqc.html’
Pre compiled FastQC reports are also available here
A reminder of what each section means can be found in the FastQC docs
Feel free to look through these but it’s generally easier to aggregate our reports into one, we can do with with MultiQC.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
MultiQC
MultiQC provides a simple way to combine the results from multiple FastQC analyses into a single report, allowing you to assess the overall quality of a study and easily identify samples that may require further investigation.
MultiQC is straightforward to use and can summarise results from dozens or even hundreds of samples in a single, easy-to-navigate report. It can also aggregate reports from multiple different tools, for example Fastq Screen for contamination, see previous workshop for more details on this.
Run Multiqc while still in the fastq directory to combine the FastQC reports from all samples.
multiqc .
You might need to refresh your browser to see this in the same space as your individual FastQC reports.
Look through the report(s) and discuss what needs to be done.
A Pre-processed MultiQC report is available here.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
Trimming
There are multiple trimming tools available, today we will use Trim Galore, this is actually a wrapper for Cutadapt, see also Trimmomatic. If you plan to do a lot of short read analysis it is definitely worth familiarising yourself with Cutadapt.
There are several different means of trimming data, by quality, length or by specific adapter sequence (or all of the above), this is carried out in a specific order. First reads are trimmed based on our chosen quality filter, then for adapter contamination and finally any reads below our minimum length are discarded.
Trim Galore selects the correct adapter sequence for us, we are selecting a minimum phred quality of 20 and length of 20bp and a stringency of 3 which means atleast 3 bases must match our adapter sequence before trimming. The cores argument determines how many CPUs are used, it is able to handle all samples in one command.
trim_galore --cores 4 --fastqc -q 20 --length 20 \
  --stringency 3 \
  CTCF_Rep1.fastq.gz \
  CTCF_Rep2.fastq.gz \
  Input_Control.fastq.gz
This generates new ‘trimmed’ FASTQ files as well as text reports (ending ’_trimming_report.txt’) but also runs FastQC for us on the trimmed data.
Reports can be viewed as text files;
less fastq/CTCF_Rep1.fastq.gz_trimming_report.txt

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
QC on Trimmed Data
Once we have performed the trimming it’s a good idea to re-run our FastQC and MultiQC to make sure the trimmed data is as expected and resolves any issues.
We can re-run MultiQC while adding the -f (force) argument to override our previous report and –fullnames to not clean our sample names and include the trimmed data.
multiqc --fullnames -f .
Link to updated MultiQC report
Individual pre-compiled FastQC reports are also available here
Hopefully the cleaned data is now passing each section or atleast receiving a warning rather than a fail. Note I have subsampled a GC rich chromosome. Remember these tests are not absolute and depend on the specific data.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
Aligning reads
Now that we have our trimmed data, we can align our reads to our reference genome, we will use GRCh38/hg38, references are built from FASTA sequence files.
We already have the relevant reference FASTA file available on the server, this also includes indexes needed for the main alignment tools, these are required for the running of most tools.
If running on your own machine this can be obtained via;
wget http://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/bigZips/hg38.fa.gz
gunzip hg38.fa.gz
Today we will use bowtie2 but there are several popular short read alignment tools available (BWA, miniMap2 etc.), these are generally interchangeable but for RNA-seq experiments it is strongly recommended to use STAR as it is splice aware.
We will point to the relevant index file but for reference this was created with;
### do not run
#bowtie2-build -f /home/genomes/human/hg38/hg38.fa hg38
###
Lets create a bowtie2 output directory just for our alignments;
cd ..
mkdir bt2_out
Assuming this index exists we can run the alignment with these commands, we are running each sample one by one, this will take a little while.

-p Processors (threads)
-x Basename of the genome index
-U Unpaired data
-S Output in SAM format

With 2> we are redirecting output to a log file
# Rep 1
bowtie2 -p 4 -x /home/genomes/human/hg38/bowtie2_indexes/hg38 -U fastq/CTCF_Rep1_trimmed.fq.gz -S bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.sam 2> bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1_bowtie2.log

# Rep 2
bowtie2 -p 4 -x /home/genomes/human/hg38/bowtie2_indexes/hg38 -U fastq/CTCF_Rep2_trimmed.fq.gz -S bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.sam 2> bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2_bowtie2.log

# Input Control
bowtie2 -p 4 -x /home/genomes/human/hg38/bowtie2_indexes/hg38 -U fastq/Input_Control_trimmed.fq.gz -S bt2_out/Input_Control.sam 2> bt2_out/Input_Control_bowtie2.log
The output alignments are in the Sequence Alignment/Map (SAM) format, generally we can output/convert directly into the compressed ‘binary’ BAM format but lets take a closer look at the SAM files.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
SAM Format
Sequence Alignment/Map (SAM) files contain our alignment positions as well as columns contaning information on the quality of the alignment, mismatches, the number of times a read mapped, mapping of paired ends and other custom flags and statistics.
See the Docs for the full specification.
[SAM diagram here] NEED TO ADD THIS
Let’s take a look at one of our SAM files.
samtools view  bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.sam | less
Each alignment contains a SAM flag which encodes information, this can be used for downstream filtering or reporting.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
SAMTOOLS
Samtools is a powerful tool for working with SAM/BAM files.
Here we are sorting our SAM alignments into the compressed BAM format, and also indexing the BAM files as downstream tools require this.

-@ specifices threads/CPUs
-o Output is specified as a parameter

# Rep 1
samtools sort -@ 4 -o bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bam bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.sam
samtools index bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bam

# Rep 2
samtools sort -@ 4 -o bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bam bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.sam
samtools index bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bam

# Input Control
samtools sort -@ 4 -o bt2_out/Input_Control.bam bt2_out/Input_Control.sam
samtools index bt2_out/Input_Control.bam
Samtools Flagstat summarises the mapping rate for reads
samtools flagstat bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bam
We can see there are 779,426 reads, 770,259 of which mapped.
Let’s confirm how many are unmapped, here we are filtering (-f) using the samflag for unmapped (04) and counting (-c) with samtools view
samtools view -c -f 4 bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bam
We should see 9,167 are unmapped, this was actually in our Bowtie2 log


 Challenge:

How many reads mapped to replicate 2?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

You could use; samtools flagstat bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bam
653498
Or being clever you could count excluding unmapped flag with ‘-F’ rather an ‘-f’
samtools view -c -F 4 bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bam
Also you check the bowtie2 logs; less bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2_bowtie2.log



We can look at where our reads align with idxstats;
samtools idxstats bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bam | grep -E '^chr[0-9XYM]+\b'
There are a lot of additional chromosomes contigs here so we’re just filtering out the main ones.
The fist column is the chromosome, the second is its size and the third is the number of mapped reads, can you tell which chromosome has the most mapped reads?

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
Coverage Tracks
Technically we can view our BAM files in a genome browser (right down to the individual base calls), but despite being compressed these files are still large and not easily view-able, they simply contain all of our alignments so make no account for sequencing depth. We want to convert our BAMs into a binned format so we can view it as a coverage track.
Bedgraph files are human readable and contain continuous coordinate data with value scores, BigWig contain the same information in compressed binary format and are excellent for genome browsers.
To create out bigWig tracks we are using bamCoverage which is a part of the DeepTools package of tools.
Multiple methods of normalization as available, here we are using Bins Per Million (BPM) to handle read depth, we are selecting a bin or window size of 10.
bamCoverage \
  -b bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1_filtered.bam \
  -o bt2_out/CTCF_Rep1.bw \
  --binSize 10 \
  --normalizeUsing BPM \
  --numberOfProcessors 4

bamCoverage -b bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2_filtered.bam -o bt2_out/CTCF_Rep2.bw --binSize 10 --normalizeUsing BPM --numberOfProcessors 4
bamCoverage -b bt2_out/Input_Control_filtered.bam -o bt2_out/Input_Control.bw --binSize 10 --normalizeUsing BPM --numberOfProcessors 4
In the next section we will visualise our bigWig files in IGV, it is also possible to upload your tracks to online genome browsers such as UCSC, ensembl or the IGV web app.


 Key points


How to assess FASTQ quality
When and what to Trim
Align to the correct reference
Alignments are in SAM/BAM format
Filtering based on SAM Flags and MAPQ Scores
Coverage Track formats

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
ChIP-seq
ChIP-seq (Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing) is a lab based method to identify DNA-binding regions of specific proteins, often looking at either histone modifications or transcription factor binding sites, while the initial steps for these are the same, peak calling and downstream analysis will differ.

title: HTS data analysis (ChIP-seq)
text:
Optional Exercise

If performing peak calling consider whether broad peak calling more appropriate. If interested in RNA-Seq analyis see this previous workshop, please note it won’t be possible to follow this exactly as it was designed for a specific system but the steps taken will be the same.
